isc2.cc.d2.incident-response::gate.note: I hesitated between B and E first: the prompt says encryption is already spreading on the shared drive, so shutting off the drive (E) feels as urgent as isolating the workstation (B). B-first holds up because it cuts the source and keeps memory evidence, but E-first is a tempting answer for a novice. The order D before A, then C, was clear.

isc2.cc.d2.incident-response::isc2.cc.d2.note: For blank 3 a learner might write 'the plan' or 'playbooks', since the lesson says the review decides 'what changes in the plan'. The grader should accept those or expect 'Preparation' only.

Statement 7 ('record how long detection took') has the word 'detection' in it, which could pull a careless learner toward Detection & analysis. The phrase 'to measure improvement' does steer it to Post-incident.

isc2.cc.d2.incident-response::isc2.cc.d2.answer: The four phases are Preparation, Detection and analysis, Containment-eradication-recovery, and Post-incident activity. You contain first because cutting a compromised machine off the network stops the attack spreading and stops the attacker controlling it while you work. If you cleaned or restored while the attacker was still active, they could just get back in. You keep the machine powered on because its memory holds running processes and live connections, and that evidence is lost when the power goes. A playbook is a written plan for one type of incident, such as ransomware or a lost laptop, made of concrete steps with named owners. The lessons learned in the post-incident review feed back into Preparation, improving the plan and the playbooks.

isc2.cc.d3.least-privilege::isc2.cc.d3.l.note: Statement 6 ('Run the monthly payroll report') is not covered by the job as described, which is only processing approved salary changes. Under the least-privilege lesson a careful learner could reasonably say Remove it. Either add report-running to the job description or drop the statement.

isc2.cc.d3.least-privilege::isc2.cc.d3.l.answer: Least privilege means every account, whether a person, service or script, gets only the minimum access its job needs. Need-to-know applies the same idea to information: even someone who is cleared only sees the records their work requires. Blast radius is how much damage a stolen account can do. The attacker can reach exactly what the account could, so a tightly scoped account limits the harm. Privilege creep happens when people change roles and keep their old access, so it piles up over the years. Regular access reviews fix it by removing what is no longer needed. The right to delete audit logs is especially dangerous because it lets someone erase the record of what they did. That breaks separation of duties and hides an attack.

isc2.cc.d4.subnetting::gate.note: The prompt says the answers must be right 'with no hint', yet the gate offers two hints. A learner cannot tell whether revealing a hint fails the gate outright or only lowers the score, and 'the time allowed' is never stated.

isc2.cc.d4.subnetting::isc2.cc.d4.subnet.answer: Subtract the prefix from 32 to get the host bits. For /25 to /30 all the work happens in the last octet. Find the mask value in that octet (128, 192, 224, 240, 248 or 252), then subtract it from 256 to get the block size. Subnets start at multiples of the block size. The network address is the multiple at or just below your address, with all host bits 0. The broadcast address is the next multiple minus one, with all host bits 1. The usable host count is 2 to the power of the host bits, minus 2. Those two addresses cannot be given to a device because the network address identifies the subnet itself and the broadcast address reaches every host on it.
isc2.cc.d4.subnetting::isc2.cc.d4.subnet.note: The lesson says the network and broadcast addresses 'cannot be given to a device' but never says why. This prompt asks the learner to explain why, so a learner limited to the reading cannot answer it. Add one sentence to the lesson: the first address identifies the subnet and the last reaches every host.

isc2.cc.d5.security-awareness::gate.note: I hesitated on 8 (no-reply@calendar.yourcompany.com) against 4 (yourcompany.com.mailbox-support.io). The lesson never teaches that the domain is read from the right, so without hint0 a novice could mark 8 as Phishing or 4 as Legitimate. Separately, every phishing line also makes a bad request, so the request cue alone gets all ten right and the address-reading skill is never tested on its own.

isc2.cc.d5.security-awareness::isc2.cc.d.answer: Three forms of social engineering are phishing by email (including spear phishing and whaling), vishing by phone call, and pretexting, where a made-up story makes a request seem normal. They rely on urgency, authority, secrecy and requests that skip the normal process. To check a suspicious message, first look at the real sender address rather than the display name. Then ask what it wants, and whether that request would normally arrive this way. Verify through a channel you already know, such as the directory phone number, and report it quickly. For passwords, NIST favours long passphrases over forced complexity and a different password for every site, kept in a password manager. Turn on MFA, and change a password only when it may have been exposed.

isc2.cc.d5.logging-monitoring::gate.note: This is straightforward. The lesson stresses checking whether any attempt from the source succeeded, but the gate does not ask it. Here none did, since the accepted logins are from 10.0.0.5, so a fifth blank on that would test the most important question.

isc2.cc.d5.logging-monitoring::isc2.cc.d.answer: Worth logging are sign-ins that succeed and fail with their source, privilege changes such as new accounts or admin group additions, configuration changes, access to sensitive data, and security tool alerts. A SIEM collects logs from across the organisation, normalises them into one format, correlates events from different sources and raises alerts when a rule matches. Clocks must be synchronised to one time source, or events cannot be put in order. Logs must be sent to a separate, protected store so an intruder with admin rights cannot delete the evidence. For a suspected brute-force attack I would find where the attempts came from, how many there were, which accounts were tried and over what time span. Then I would check whether any attempt from that source succeeded.

isc2.cc.d2.incident-response::hint0.note: This gives a reversibility test that sorts containment ahead of eradication and recovery, so the learner reasons about the order instead of recalling it. It does not settle B against E.
